1.pericope_label: A three-year famine traced to Saul’s slaughter of the Gibeonites, who ask for seven of his sons

schools.summary: Henry holds that Saul acted under colour of zeal for Israel’s honour, that he might seem wiser than the judges before him, and perhaps meant it for an instance of royal prerogative, the power to disannul the most solemn leagues; it may be he designed this severity to atone for his clemency towards the Amalekites. What made the sin exceedingly great was that he not only shed innocent blood but therein violated the oath by which the nation was bound. On the delay he will not have the question pressed, since God’s judgments often look a great way back and there is no statute of limitation to be pleaded against God’s demands; it is not for us to object against a people smarting for the sin of their king, since perhaps they were aiding and abetting. On the Gibeonites’ terms he observes that money is no satisfaction for blood, that those over-value money and under-value life who sell their relations’ blood for corruptible things, and that they had a fair opportunity to demand discharge from their servitude and did not take it, since though the covenant was broken on the other side it should not be broken on theirs.

Gill reports the case for displacement with its grounds but leaves it open, noting that one Jewish writing dates these events to the year after Saul was slain while other copies of the same book say thirty years after, and that Abarbinel and some of the best chronologers hold the order as it stands.

Ellicott would read simply and there was, there being no indication of time in the original, and finds the phrase in the days of David purposely indefinite; from the sparing of Mephibosheth the events must fall after David knew him, and if an earlier reproach alludes to this execution, before Absalom’s revolt. He adds that the narrative is omitted from Chronicles, and that a famine in Palestine always followed deficient winter rains and was not uncommon, though three successive years was alarming enough to suggest a particular cause. On the two questions usually asked — why the punishment was so long delayed and why it fell on David’s people — he answers both nationally: Saul slew the Gibeonites not as the son of Kish but as king of Israel, involving all Israel in the violation of the national oath, so that until the evil were put away all Israel must suffer, and the lesson of the nation’s continued responsibility from age to age was greatly enhanced by the delay. He judges Saul’s zeal itself of the same ungodly character as much else in that reign, pride and self-will cloaked under a care for God’s honour, and notes that money compensation for blood, common among ancient nations, was forbidden in the law of Israel, which these Gibeonites appear to have accepted. Keil and Delitzsch place the whole episode among the matters appended to the close of the reign, and explain the Gibeonites’ refusal of silver and gold as a refusal to take any pecuniary payment for the blood shed among them.

Wesley argues hardest for displacement, holding with the best interpreters that these things were done long before Absalom’s rebellion: Saul’s sin would not have lain unpunished so long, nor the bones of Saul and Jonathan gone unmoved, and David in old age attempting a giant, or his people suffering him to, is improbable; the matters stand here because David’s sin being once related it was convenient that his punishments should immediately succeed, which is frequent in scripture-story. He describes Saul’s method as seeking to cut the Gibeonites off with some colour of justice, aggravating their faults and oppressing them with excessive labours, intending by degrees to wear them out. Clarke makes the silence the difficulty instead of the order: of this famine we know nothing, and no such fact as the slaying of the Gibeonites appears in Saul’s life or anywhere else in Scripture. He alone objects to the procedure itself, that it is very strange a choice of this kind should be left to such a people, and asks why it was not asked of God himself.

10.pericope_label: Rizpah watches over the bodies until the rain, and David gathers the bones of Saul’s house for burial

schools.summary: Henry meets the difficulty of the bodies being left hanging against the law requiring burial the same day. He reports that one of the Jewish rabbin wished the passage expunged, that God’s name might be sanctified, thinking it dishonoured by his accepting a breach of his own law; but the case was extraordinary, and the very reason for the law is the reason for the exception, since he that is left hanging is accursed, so that ordinary malefactors must not be so used and these must, being sacrificed not to the justice of the nation but for its crime. On Rizpah he notes her restraint, that she might have cited the divine law to bear her out yet neither steals nor forces away the bodies but patiently submits and pitches her tent near the gibbets; and he divides her conduct in two, that in indulging her grief she did as mourners are too apt to do, to no good purpose, while in testifying her love she let the world know her sons died for no sin of their own but for their father’s. He assumes the shorter reckoning of her watch without arguing it, supposing the rain came perhaps not many days after the hanging, and adds the dignity of the burial, that royal dust should not be lost in the graves of the common people.

Gill reads the sackcloth practically as well as mournfully, a token of grief and the fittest defence against the weather, heat by day and cold by night. On the report reaching David he will not guess whether it was told out of good will or ill, but observes that it was not disagreeable to him, serving to move his pity and to show that the execution had been obedience and not personal revenge.

Keil and Delitzsch say that when Rizpah’s touching care for the dead was told David, he saw the bones of the whole fallen royal house buried in the family grave at Zela. Ellicott adds the second motive, that David wished to show no enmity against the house of Saul. On the apparent clash between the wall of Bethshan in the earlier account and the street from which the men of Jabesh took the bodies, both deny any contradiction, since the open place of an eastern town is not in its middle but a broad square just inside the gate where the people were wont to gather.

Clarke uses this scene to deny the whole transaction. Did God require this sacrifice of Saul’s sons, he asks, probably all innocent of their father’s alleged crime? Was the requisition of the Gibeonites to be considered an oracle of God? Certainly not: God will not have man’s blood for sacrifice, no more than he will have swine’s blood, and the famine might have been removed by the sacrifices prescribed in the law and a general humiliation of the people. On the length of Rizpah’s watch he holds the rain must be the periodical autumn rains, which commence about October, and recoils at the arithmetic, asking whether this broken-hearted woman could have watched the bodies, probably in the open air, more than five months; he rejects the alternative, that the rain was the mere breaking of the drought soon after the execution, as not agreeing with the way the account dates her watch from the beginning of harvest. Wesley has David hear of her vigil with such approbation that he thought fit to imitate her piety, being provoked by her example to do what he had hitherto neglected, that the honour done the dead might comfort this disconsolate widow; and he gives Henry’s judgment on her motive in almost the same words.

15.pericope_label: War with the Philistines again; David waxes faint, Abishai rescues him, and his men swear he shall not go out

schools.summary: Henry praises the going out, that David, though old, desired no writ of ease from the public service but went in person, which shows he fought not for his own glory, being already loaded with glory and needing no more, but for the good of his kingdom. Then he marks the failure: David thought he could bear the fatigues of war as formerly, and his will was good, but he found himself deceived, for age had cut his hair, and after a little toil he waxed faint; the champion was soon aware of the advantage and thought to slay him, but God was not in his thoughts, and in that very day they all perished, for there is no strength, nor counsel, nor confidence against the Lord. On the rescue he reads David and not Abishai as the one who struck the blow, grounding it on the chapter’s closing notice that David had a hand in slaying the giants, and takes Abishai’s part to have been the succour, a cordial to relieve his fainting spirits or the office of a second. He calls David the guide and glory of Israel, says the oath was resolved in council to keep that light from ever again being put in hazard of being blown out, and draws the rule that the lives of those as valuable to their country as David was ought to be preserved with a double care, by themselves and by others.

Gill asks only whether the phrase sons of the giant means Goliath’s own sons or the race in general, and attributes the renewed Philistine wars partly to the number of giants among them and partly to the decline of David’s life.

Keil and Delitzsch say flatly that Abishai came to the king’s help and slew the giant. They take the giant’s name as a genuine proper name rather than a man of Nob, probably meaning that his dwelling is on the height, a name he may have had from an inaccessible castle, and they trace him to the tribe-father of the Rephaim, of whom only a few families survived even in the time of Moses. They also explain the title given to David, that Jehovah was his light and had lighted his lamp and enlightened his darkness. Ellicott states the ambiguity of the rescue rather than resolving it: the original leaves it doubtful whether Abishai is the subject of the verb or whether it should be simply he, referring to David, and the closing notice does seem to imply that one of the sons of the giant at least fell by David’s own hand. On the name he thinks some error has crept into the text, grants that no proposed emendation is free from difficulty, and gives as the likeliest the Speaker’s Commentary’s, which reads they halted for the first element and, by a change of a single letter, at Gob for the second, yielding a text running David waxed faint, and they halted at Gob, and there was a man which was of the sons of the giant — a reading he supports from the next verses, which seem to presuppose an earlier battle at Gob.

Clarke notes that David’s fainting is recorded nowhere else, and that the parallel passage in Chronicles does not mention this war at all. On the oath he takes the lamp as the emblem of direction and support, David being the light by which all Israel was guided and without whom the nation must be involved in darkness, and he cites a line of Homer using light in the same sense, of one who had failed to be a light to Patroclus and his companions.

18.pericope_label: Four more giants of Gath fall to David’s servants, and Clarke indicts the chapter’s whole text

schools.summary: Henry alone treats the four combats as one lesson. The giants were probably the remains of the sons of Anak, who though long feared fell at last, and he notes of the last that having seen the others fall he defied Israel still. From this he draws three things: that it is folly for the strong man to glory in his strength, since David’s servants were no bigger than other men yet by divine assistance mastered one giant after another, God choosing by the weak things to confound the mighty; that the terror of the mighty in the land of the living commonly goes down slain to the pit; and that the most powerful enemies are often reserved for the last conflict, David having begun his glory with one giant and concluded it with four — for death is a Christian’s last enemy and a son of Anak, yet through him that triumphed for us we hope to be more than conquerors even over that enemy. On the slayer of the last giant he says he would have taken him for the wily Jonadab but that the one was noted for subtlety and this Jonathan for bravery.

Gill will not have these giants born to Goliath, since one of them was his brother, but to some giant of Gath, and reports the Greek naming their family Repha, which Abarbinel takes for a woman among the daughters of the giants and the Talmudists identify with Orpah; he holds them descendants of the Anakim left in Gath after Joshua.

Keil and Delitzsch reach the same mechanism as Clarke on the Elhanan verse, that the word for weavers crept in from the next line through a copyist’s oversight, and report the division among commentators, most holding the text of Chronicles original and this one corrupt, others the reverse. On the scene of the first battle they note it is called Gob here and Gezer in Chronicles, reject Thenius’s view that Gob is a slip of the pen since it occurs again, and suggest a small place near Gezer. Ellicott agrees the word for weavers crept in from the line below, observes that the words the brother of are not in the Hebrew here but supplied from Chronicles, and preserves a curious Jewish tradition that this Elhanan was David himself, the Chaldee paraphrasing it as David the son of Jesse, the weaver of veils for the sanctuary, who was of Bethlehem, slew Goliath the Gittite. He thinks it not at all remarkable that the names of small places should be lost after three thousand years, makes the slayer of the last giant David’s nephew and probably the brother of the wily Jonadab, and remarks that David’s family connections seem to have made up a clan of heroes.

Clarke gathers his objections here into a twelve-point indictment of the chapter itself. The three-year famine is spoken of nowhere else and was too remarkable to omit; Saul’s attempt on the Gibeonites is nowhere else mentioned and was such a breach of the national faith as could scarcely have failed to raise an insurrection; that seven innocent men should hang for an offending father seems inconsistent with justice and mercy; Rizpah’s months of watching are very improbable as related; and the long hanging was against an express law which God did not command a breach of. His conclusion is unguarded: it seems as if a Gibeonite has had a hand in the copies that have come down to us, or the first fourteen verses were inserted from a less authentic document, and till he gets further light he concludes that the whole chapter is not now what it would be from the pen of an inspired writer — though he insists even so that the great foundation of God stands sure. On the Elhanan verse in particular he calls it a most manifest corruption, since David and not Elhanan slew Goliath, notes that our translators borrowed words from Chronicles to make the two agree, and accounts for it by supposing the word for weavers slipped from one line into the other and the Bethlehemite is a corruption of the giant’s name.
